| [THEORY-079](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-079.md) v3 | Bayesian model reduction under the Laplace approximation prices the reductions of a singular parent model with a Gaussian Occam factor, so its free-energy differences can be wrong by a term that grows with log n | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. BMR's closed form (Friston & Penny, [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 9; Friston, Parr & Zeidman, [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md), Eq. 11) charges a reduction through log-determinants of Gaussian precisions, which is MacKay's regular Occam factor. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), says that models with hierarchical layers or hidden variables are singular, that no normal distribution approximates their posterior, and that their free energy grows as λ log n. BMR is applied to exactly such models: mixtures, hierarchical empirical Bayes and latent states. Neither literature cites the other. The exact identity is untouched ([THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md)). The claim is about its Laplace form, and a test on reduced-rank regression would settle it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-080](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-080.md) v4 | In a linearised network with a Gaussian prior on its parameters, the Occam factor is a sum over the NTK's eigenvalues, so on spherical data each harmonic pays ½ log(1 + βnµ_k/α) and the kernel's eigenvalue decay schedules the complexity penalty across frequencies | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. Its exact half is filed as the record's own claim, CLAIM-384; what stays here is the spherical account. A network linearised at initialisation, with an isotropic Gaussian prior on its parameters and Gaussian noise, is MacKay's linear-in-parameters model ([LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md)). Its Occam factor is −½ Σ log(1 + βλ_a/α) over the eigenvalues of JᵀJ. These are the empirical NTK's, which on uniform spherical data form Bietti & Bach's degree blocks, nµ_k with multiplicity N(d, k) ([LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md)). Degrees whose βnµ_k exceeds α pay about ½ log n per harmonic, and degrees below pay almost nothing. With µ_k ~ k^(−d), the number of paid directions γ grows as n^((d−1)/d), not as the parameter count. Basri et al.'s bound ([LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md), Eq. 14) is the matching data-fit term. The kernel's decay exponent is the schedule of the penalty. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md) v2 | The evidence of any model formed from a full model by changing only its prior is the full evidence times the full posterior expectation of the prior ratio, so the Savage–Dickey ratio is its point-mass case and choosing which parameters to keep is evidence maximisation over the prior | Friston & Penny (2011), [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 3: if models share a likelihood and differ only in priors nested inside a full prior, then p(y\|m_i) = p(y\|m_F)·E_{p(θ\|y,m_F)}[p_i(θ)/p_F(θ)]. Their Eq. 6 is the point-mass case, the Savage–Dickey ratio that Wagenmakers et al. (2010), [LIT-609](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-609.md), derive from the other end, and that Dickey (1971), LIT-610, stated in this form for any continuous likelihood. Friston, Parr & Zeidman, [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md), restate it for any new prior and give conjugate closed forms. Active because the identity is three lines of Bayes' rule that anyone can check. The two Savage–Dickey conditions turn out to be the same condition. The identity is exact. Its Laplace and variational forms are only as good as the full posterior, and with no constraint on the prior family the optimum is maximum likelihood. | Active |
| [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md) v4 | The Bayesian complexity penalty grows as (d/2) log n in a regular model, where the curvature at the optimum sets the Occam factor, and as λ log n in a singular one, where λ is the real log canonical threshold; with the prior positive on the optimal set, λ falls below d/2 when that set is infinite or has a point of degenerate curvature, and equals d/2 when it is finitely many points of non-degenerate curvature | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), writes the evidence as best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible volume, which under a Gaussian approximation is P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A. When the likelihood dominates, det A grows as n^d, so the penalty is (d/2) log n. Watanabe's WBIC paper, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), recovers that case (Lemma 3, Theorem 5) and states what replaces it when the Fisher information is degenerate at the optimum: λ log n − (m − 1) log log n, with λ the RLCT (Theorem 2). The regular half is re-derived by Laplace's method with its conditions. The singular half is Watanabe's cited theorem, checked by exact free energies in two singular models of known λ. The volume reading of λ is in Watanabe's book, which is unread. | Active |
| [THEORY-259](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-259.md) v3 | For a recursive family of likelihoods and the universal prior, the Bayesian two-part code length −log Pr(D\|H) − log m(H) equals the ideal-MDL length K(D\|H) + K(H) plus the randomness deficiency of D for H, up to a constant fixed by the family; so ideal MDL and MAP selection agree to within a constant among hypotheses for which the data are random, and can part where they are not | Vitányi & Li (1999/2000), [LIT-225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-225.md), read in [NOTE-801](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-801.md). With the universal prior m and a recursive family Pr(·\|·), −log Pr(D\|H) − log m(H) = K(D\|H) + K(H) + d(D\|H) + O(1), where d(D\|H) = log(m(D\|H)/Pr(D\|H)) is the universal randomness deficiency of D for H; d ≥ −K(Pr(·\|·)) − O(1), and d is bounded exactly when D is Martin-Löf random for H. So ideal MDL and MAP agree to within a constant on admissible hypotheses (Theorems 3–5, re-derived by the record) and part where the data are not random for the hypothesis (0ⁿ against the fair coin). The paper's slack α = K(Pr(·\|H)) + K(P) is an upper bound, not the gap. | Active |

| [THEORY-624](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-624.md) v3 | Orseau, McGill and Legg cast whether an identified system is an agent or a device as Bayesian model comparison between descriptions of the function it optimises and descriptions of its input-output mapping, so that the verdict is relative to the observer's prior; on seven toy gridworld trajectories goal-seeking comes out agent-like and wall-following device-like, and they argue that under a speed prior everything may look like an agent | Orseau, McGill & Legg (2018), [LIT-911](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-911.md), read in [NOTE-705](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-705.md). | [THEORY-718](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-718.md) | In a linear-in-parameters model with Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior, the evidence is exactly the best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor set by the posterior curvature, and when the design grows linearly with n that factor costs (k/2) log n | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), Eqs. 5–6 with Eqs. 16 and 19–20, read in [NOTE-471](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-471.md): for y = Φw + noise with Gaussian noise of precision β and the prior w ~ N(0, α⁻¹I) on k weights, the posterior is exactly Gaussian, so the evidence is exactly P(D\|w_MP) times the Occam factor P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A, with A = αI + βΦᵀΦ. If ΦᵀΦ/n converges to a positive-definite matrix and w_MP stays bounded, the log Occam factor is −(k/2) log n + O(1). Exact for this model class only. The general regular case and the singular case are [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md), which is Proposed. | Active |

| [THEORY-2237](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2237.md) | Schuhr finds in a laboratory experiment with real money that intertemporal choices presented as a free series of two or three paired decisions, chosen at once, are more patient in their first choices than the same choices presented singly, and that forcing the paired decisions to match lowers patient choice, which he reads as reward bundling done by the chooser rather than imposed | Schuhr (2015), [LIT-3114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-3114.md), read in part in [NOTE-2327](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2327.md) for [LEAD-078](../../../record/leads.d/LEAD-078.md). In eight one-session treatments of about thirty students each, a free series of decisions raised the mixture probability of exponential discounting by 0.307 (p = 0.019), forcing the decisions together lowered it by 0.330, and stake size did not explain it.
